evidence.claim: Above downtown Pittsburgh, the byway links overlooks and surviving hillside inclines.
evidence.quote: The byway features views of downtown Pittsburgh and provides access to sites such as the Monongahela Incline, the Duquesne Incline, and the Mount Washington overlook.

evidence.claim: Grand View Scenic Byway takes in Pittsburgh’s Grandview Avenue, P.J. McArdle Roadway and Sycamore Street.
evidence.quote: The Grand View Scenic Byway runs along Grandview Avenue, P.J. McArdle Roadway, and Sycamore Street in Pittsburgh, Allegheny County.

evidence.claim: Visit Pennsylvania highlights its views of downtown and access to the Mount Washington overlook and two inclines.
evidence.quote: The byway features views of downtown Pittsburgh and provides access to sites such as the Monongahela Incline, the Duquesne Incline, and the Mount Washington overlook.

evidence.claim: The corridor became a Pennsylvania byway in 2003.
evidence.quote: GRAND VIEW Effective: 2003 District: 11-0 City: Pittsburgh Routes: Avenue, Roadway and Street Grandview Avenue, McCardle Roadway and Sycamore Street in Pittsburgh.

evidence.claim: Reaching this hillside was once a problem for the people who lived on it.
evidence.quote: Travel between the "hill" and other areas was hindered by the steep terrain and a lack of public transport or good roads.

evidence.claim: In the 1860s, industry occupied most of the flat ground along the Monongahela’s south bank, pushing housing onto Mount Washington’s steep slopes.
evidence.quote: industry occupied most of the flat lands adjacent to the south bank of the Monongahela River, leaving only the steep, surrounding hillsides of Mount Washington, or "Coal Hill", for housing.

evidence.claim: German immigrants proposed cable inclines, and the Monongahela passenger line opened in 1870.
evidence.quote: The German immigrants who settled on Mt. Washington, remembering the Seilbahnen (cable cars) of their former country, proposed construction of inclines along the face of Coal Hill.

evidence.claim: As roads multiplied and car use grew in the twentieth century, most inclines closed; by the late 1960s, only the Monongahela and Duquesne remained in operation.
evidence.quote: But as more roads were built in the twentieth century on "Coal Hill", as it was known, and automobile use increased, most of the other inclines were closed. By the end of the 1960s, only the Monongahela Incline and the Duquesne Incline remained in operation.

evidence.claim: For an east-to-west sequence of stops, begin with the Monongahela Incline and continue to the Duquesne Incline, where an observation deck faces Pittsburgh’s Golden Triangle.
evidence.quote: An observation deck was added at the top affording a view of Pittsburgh's "Golden Triangle".

evidence.quote: Prussian-born engineer John Endres of Cincinnati was commissioned to design the Monongahela Incline, which opened on May 28, 1870, as the first for passenger use.

evidence.claim: A larger freight incline opened beside it in 1884 and operated until 1935.
evidence.quote: this incline was built beside the smaller, original Monongahela Incline and opened in 1884.

evidence.claim: That neighboring line could carry vehicles as well as people; its concrete pylons remain visible during the passenger incline’s descent.
evidence.quote: It had a unique 10 ft (3,048 mm) broad gauge that would allow vehicles, as well as walk-on passengers, to ascend and descend the hill.

evidence.claim: The Duquesne Incline closed in 1962 with major repairs needed and few passengers.
evidence.quote: In 1962, the Duquesne Incline was closed, apparently for good. Major repairs were needed, and with so few patrons, the incline's private owners did little.

evidence.claim: Duquesne Heights residents raised money to restore it, and a nonprofit reopened the line on July 1, 1963.
evidence.quote: But local Duquesne Heights residents launched a fund-raiser to help restore the incline. It was a huge success, and on July 1, 1963, the incline reopened under the auspices of a non-profit organization dedicated to its preservation.

evidence.claim: Samuel Diescher’s incline had been completed in 1877, originally powered by steam.
evidence.quote: Originally steam powered, the Duquesne Incline was designed by Samuel Diescher, a Hungarian-American civil engineer based in Pittsburgh, and completed in 1877.

evidence.claim: Its later refurbishment exposed the original wood of the cars built by Philadelphia’s J. G. Brill and Company.
evidence.quote: The cars, built by the J. G. Brill and Company of Philadelphia, have been stripped of paint to reveal the original wood.
